newsitem.title: UK: British farmers told they need EU support.
newsitem.headline: British farmers told they need EU support.

text.p: British farmers, currently benefiting from good production and the fall in the value of sterling after it left the EU's exchange rate mechanism, should not be too quick to assume that they can do without the support of the CAP, according to Essex farmer Guy Smith.

The feeling of most British farmers over the last few years is that the CAP (Common Agricultural Policy) seems so generous in its handouts that it cannot last in its present form, Smith said in a paper presented to the Oxford Farming Conference.

But he reckoned the CAP had more staying power. And he advised British farmers to remember that the average UK cereal yield in the past ten years had been 2.6 tonnes to the acre and the average world market price over the same period had been 80 stg per tonne. This gives a gross return of 200 stg per acre.
"As a farmer of above average size I could cut my overheads," Smith said. "The only way I could compete with the Americans is to adopt their strategies of production," he said.
But he described the chances of survival of his 200 acre neighbour as "less than slim."
A cut in subsidies could mean an agriculture with fewer farmers, Smith said. They would be "custodians of the countryside with no money to take care of the countryside."
